The adjutant-general to-day addressed the following to the governor: "The rapid and healthful growth of public sentiment in favor of law and order along our western frontier, and the inclination of the people to adopt the peaceful practices and methods which are lawful and common in other sections in the state, have placed many of these extreme western counties in a condition, politically and socially, to enable them to be brought under the operation of the penal statute, commonly known as the pistol law; and I would therefore respectfully ask that your excellency, in order to encourage this salutary spirit among the people, and to meet the open and approved wishes of some of the good citizens concerned, issue your proclamation adding the following named counties to the list of those wherein the pistol law is enforced: Howard, Martin, Crockett, Pecos, Wells and Thompson.

A conductor of the Central, who fell while boarding his train at Manor, the other day, and was so seriously injured, is improving and will get well. Three of his toes on his left foot had to be amputated and he will be a cripple for life.

The city council has granted right-of-way to the lunatic asylum and university sewer, provided the state permits the city and private individuals to make connections with it. This the state cannot accept, as it will require a much larger and more expensive sewer than it contemplated.

Two boys, aged 17 and 19 years, shot two Mexicans near Oatmanville to-day, killing one on the spot and inflicting wounds on the other that will result in death. The Mexicans had testified against a friend of the boys in a case for carrying concealed weapons. Officers are out investigating the difficulty.

A DOUBLE KILLING.
TWO MEXICANS REPORTED
SHOT AND KILLED
Near the Town of Oatmanville in this County.
The Murderers Still at Large-An Inquest to be Held To-Day.
News reached the city late yesterday afternoon of the killing, near Oatmanville, of one Mexican and the wounding of another. The first information was brought by a colored man, but he knew nothing save that the men had been shot. Learning that the killing probably had its origin in a trial in that magisterial precinct during the day, the reporter of the STATESMAN sought Mr. R. H. Brumby, who was engaged in the court as attorney for the state during said trial. He says that about ten days ago William Boston, Lewis Wade, James LaRue and another whose name he did not know or remember, were passing the house of Augustin Agirer, a Mexican, who lives on the place of Mr. Richard Young, several miles from Oatmanville; that one of them shot at Agirer's dog, and upon the latter asking why the shooting was done, Boston leveled his pistol at him, accompanied by the threat to shoot him. For this the Mexican swore out a complaint against Boston in Justice Pace's court, charging him with carrying a sixshooter and also with an assault. Yesterday the trial took place and Boston was fined twenty-five dollars. Mr. Brumby states that during the trial the parties were very bitter in their denunciation of the Mexican, and after the fine had been inflicted they threatened to take Boston from the officer who was to bring him to the city. For this latter reason a posse was summoned and Boston brought in, Wade and LaRue leaving at the same time, going in a direction from the city.

This is all Mr. B. knew about the matter, but from Mrs. Young who arrived in the city later in the day, these additional particulars were learned:

Mrs. Young was at or near her house, her husband being in the city, when the wife of Agirer came to her screaming, saying the latter had been killed. Mrs. Y. immediately went to the spot indicated, and found Agirer dead, and another Mexican, named Redel, shot in the breast, and, as she supposed, mortally wounded. Mrs. Young came at once to the city and reported the case to her husband, detailing the statements made to her by the Mexican woman, which were substantially as follows: She and her husband and Redel were on their way home from court, and when nearly to Mr. Young's house were overtaken by Wade and LaRue; that they informed Agirrer that he either had to take a whipping or die: that the latter began to beg, when LaRue without another word shot and killed him; that she ran to the house for help, and when she returned with Mrs. Young, as stated, found Redel also shot and the murderers gone.

An inquest will be held this morning, when the foregoing statements may be confirmed or refuted by the facts in the case. At this writing there is no possible way to know if they be correct, and therefore comment would be out of place. It was stated last night that a posse had gone in pursuit of the men whom it is said did the shooting.

Boston was brought to town, arranged his case and was released. Another man by the name of Madden, who came to the city in company with the colored man who first brought the news of the killing, was arrested by the police and locked up for having on a six-shooter.

STATE SPECIALS.
Austin.
Special to the Herald.
Austin, August 9.—For over six weeks the commissioner of insurance, statistics and history has had from three to six persons compiling the statistics of the state. Notwithstanding this no copy has reached the printers and the delay, it is said, is caused by unnecessary interference with and revision of the copy by Commissioner Spaight, who, it is said, assumes to correct the style and composition of well known writers of experience and acknowledged ability. Any one of the writers employed can easily compile the entire statistical report from the data furnished within four weeks. At the present rate it will be months before the work is out, and if not overbauled, corrected, and cut down by the statistical board, it will be a phenomenon in the statistical reports of the country and a useless and expensive luxury.

Prominent colored republicans here are taking active steps to secure the location at Austin of the colored branch of the state university. They will introduce in the republican state convention a resolution setting forth the advantages of this city and asking the people to vote for it.

To enforce quarantine rangers will not be furnished except to quarantine against Mexican towns. Quarantine established by towns within the interior of this state is purely a local matter for local authorities. In the opinion of the adjutant-general the state only declares and enforces quarantine on the border.

The Knights of Pity, of Bowie county, a benevolent association, filed a charter today.

The two Mexicans reported killed last night are still alive, but in a critical condition. The shooting was wholly uncalled for, the men being peaceable, industrious farmers. The men who did the shooting are still at large.

Hon. Stephen Chenault, of Orange, member of the seventeenth legislature, was married to-night to Miss Lizzie McKenzie, of this city.

A severe hail-storm passed over the eastern part of the city this afternoon. Hail-stones as large as hens' eggs fell, doing considerable damage to crops.

AUSTIN, August 10.—The commissioners of the land office received to-day from the census department the forestry bulletin. It shows the following quantity of pine timber standing in the state on May 31, 1880: Lone leaf pine, 20,308,200,000 feet; short leaf, 26,093,200,000 feet; loblolly pine, 20,907,100,000 feet. There was cut during the year ending May 31, 1880, a total of over 140,000,000 feet. Tyler, Polk and Jasper counties head the list for long leaf pine, Shelby, Cass, Bowie and Rusk for short leaf, and Houston county for loblolly.

The free schools of the state have 150,000 acres of pine land.

Mr. Kuercheer, formerly commissioner of the land office, returned to-day from Pecos county, where he has been in the interests of the Texas & Pacific railway, investigating the mines on the company's land. He found vast quantities of ore of the best quality, much of it on state lands.

The governor to-day issued a proclamation restoring the six-shooter law in the counties of Crockett, Pecos, Martin and Howard, they no longer being subject to raids by Indians.

The Waco Water company filed a resolution increasing its capital stock from $50,-000 to $100,000.

The two Mexicans shot at Oatmanville Tuesday are still alive, but both will die. Officers out to-day after the men who did the shooting returned without them and satisfied the men are still in the neighborhood provisions and whisky being furnished them by certain of their friends who have made their threats to kill any officer who attempts to make an arrest. Threats have also been made to kill the justice of the peace, who fined Boston, of the gang, for carrying a six-shooter. The citizens of Oatmanville and vicinity are afraid to do anything or give any information to officers from this city that will lead to the capture of criminals.

Governor Roberts to-day received the following telegram from Dr. Swearingen: "I go to Galveston or Indianola station. I ask not to be held in quarantine as provided by law, a right that any citizen may claim. Will you protect me? I have done my duty in the face of mobs, and will continue to do so.

[Signed] "R. M. SWEARINGEN."

The governor replied: "I will do what I can to get you home. I can't believe you will be detained after proper precaution. Telegraph me at once when you will go to Galveston so I can write them in advance."

AUSTIN, August 11.—Captain Arrington writes to the adjutant-general of troubles in the Pan Handle. Sheriff McColloch has been killed by a gambler at Tascosa, Oldham county, who was arrested by the rangers. He left five men there and recommended that they be stationed there permanently.

Colonel Loughery, who has been compiling statistics for Commissioner Spaight, leaves in the morning for Marshall. The commissioner says his statistical report will be out by December 1st.

The governor received the following telegram to-day.

NEW ORLEANS, August 11, 1881.—Governor O. M. Roberts;

The case of yellow fever in Charity hospital is a Finn, in New Orleans two and a half months, from 85 Old Levee street. Have instituted a necessary isolation. The sanitary condition of the city is good. Death rate for whites for the week ending August 5th. 19.37; deaths during the last five days, 37. No grounds for apprehension. [Signed] JOSEPH JONES, M. D. The comptroller rules that persons who manufacture peach or apple brandy must take out a liquor dealer's license. The Terrell Cotton and Woolen Manufacturing company filed a resolution increasing their capital stock from $60,000 to $200,-000. The receipts at the treasurer'soffice were $30,000.

SUICIDE AT LAMBERTVILLE, N. J.
EASTON, Penn., Aug. 14.—A resident of Lambertville, N. J., known as "Governor" Williams, who, it is said, was worth $50,000, shot himself in the stomach last evening and died this morning. He is said to have been deranged.

AN OLD OFFENDER ARRESTED.
WORCESTER, Mass., Aug. 14.—Michael J. Whalley was arrested this foreoon for attempted assault on a woman. He has lately served a sentence of eight years in prison for a similar offence and for a highway robbery committed here in 1875.

A WOMAN'S ACCIDENTAL DEATH.
WHITEHALL, N. Y., Aug. 14.—Mrs. Bushee and Miss Minnie Raynor, of Ausable Forks, were thrown from a wagon down an embankment near Keeseville this morning. Mrs. Bushee was instantly killed and Miss Raynor badly injured.

SENTENCE OF THE FORGER BRUMPTON.
PHILADELPHIA, Aug. 14.—Information has been received here that Joseph Brumpton, who was arrested in this city last summer for forgeries committed in Great Grimsby, England, was sentenced at the Lincolnshire Assizes to seven years penal servitude.

MURDERED BY HER HUSBAND.
SCRANTON, Penn., Aug. 14.—James Connors, living near Cayuga breaker in providence, quarrelled with his wife last night about money matters, and struck her on the head with a carpenter's square, inflicting injuries which have resulted fatally. Connors surrendered himself.

A RUFFIAN SHOT AND ARRESTED.
INDIANA, Penn., Aug. 14.—Duke Ray, a ruffian, after "raiding" two houses this afternoon was pursued by the sheriff and a large possse. When brought to bay he flourished a butcher-knife, and only surrendered when three bullets had been fired into his body. He is in jail, seriously wounded.

TWO MURDERERS LYNCHED.
ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 14—On Saturday night, in Chambers County, Ala., "Bole" Brooks and Charlie Griffin, convicted of the murder of one McCann a year ago, were lynched by a mob. They had been granted a new trial.

A LITTLE GIRL PROBABLY DROWNED.
TROY, N. Y., Aug. 14.—Captain F. Sanvoie, of the canal-boat G. M. Ferris, of Glens Falls, which arrived to-day from Newburg, says that on Saturday evening soon after the boat left Newburg his six-year-old daughter was missing. He believes that she fell overboard and was drowned.

Hanged by a Mob.
LAFAYETTE (Ala.), Aug. 15.—Bob Young and Charlie Griffin, colored, arrested for the murder of a white man named McCann some months ago, were hanged by a mob last night. The case was still in the courts. They protested their innocence to the last.

HUNTSVILLE, ALABAMA, SATURDAY, AUGUST 19, 1882.
LITTLE THUNDER, chief of the Chippewa Indians, died in a Chicago hospital
LITTLE THUNDER, chief of the Chippewa Indians, died in a Chicago hospital, Aug. 14. He was one of the two survivors of the Custer massacre.

BERRY WHITLEY and Robert Floyd, students at Woodville, Ga., quarreled on the 14th. Knives were drawn, and Floyd was mortally wounded.

Two cases of typhoid fever frightened all the guests from a hotel at Long Branch, N. J., and the proprietor posted a notice that he would close the establishment forthwith. Physicians said the sick men could not be removed within ten days, and the landlord consented to keep the house open that time provided he was paid $2,500 for each patient.

A NUMBER of Hebrew children were killed in a school at Grodena, Russia, the other day, by the explosion of a barrel of powder in a tradesman's house near by.

The Knights of Labor at Lonaconing, Md., counseled the tenants of companies to hold out in the strike and all necessary funds will be furnished.

M. T. BENNETT, a prominent merchant at Lebanon, Tenn., was murdered and robbed at that place on the 12th.

The County Insane Asylum at Lancaster, Pa., was totally destroyed by fire on the 13th. The inmates, 114 in number, were all saved after great exertions.

THERE was a savage prize-fight at Flushing Bay, N. Y., on the 13th. Charles Schalenbach and Robert Turnbull pounded each other into jelly for $500. Schalenbach was unconscious after the twelfth round.

THERE was a double lynching at La Fayette, Ala., the other night. Two negroes, named Bob Young and Charlie Griffin, were hanged by a mob of forty men, for the murder of a white man named McCann, some months ago. The negroes had been tried, convicted and sentenced by the Circuit Court, and the day for their execution fixed. The case was carried to the Supreme Court, and reversed, and a new trial ordered. The mob took the prisoners out of jail by force, carried them out of town, and swung them to an oak tree.

On petition of the business men of Fall River, Mass., President Arthur has granted a pardon to Joseph W. Milne, teller of the Pocasset National Bank, convicted of embezzling the funds.

As services were about to be held in the jail at Toledo, Ohio, the other day, sixteen prisoners made a break for liberty. Sheriff Harbeck knocked down two men with a jimmy, and had his eyes filled with pepper and salt. Deputy Sheriff Edgar fired a shot at a negro, which grazed his head. After a fight of three minutes the prisoners were beaten back and the door locked. An iron bar had been sawed through with a corsetsteel taken in by some woman.

At Philadelphia, Pa., on the 13th, Albert Harrison, a worthless fellow, while intoxicated, stabbed his son William, inflicting a probably fatal wound. The son interposed to protect his sister.

Three children of Mr. T. Carter, of Putman County, Ga., were burned to death on the 13th.

DOUGLAS HEATHCOTE was clubbed to death by John Goodman at Ullin, Ill., the other night.

THE CURRENT NEWS.
SOME RECENT TERRIBLE TRAGEDIES.
Wm. C. McCamus, president of the Schenectady City national bank, committed suicide by shooting himself at midnight. Ill health was probably the cause.

Edward Isom, a clerk in a store at Kerr Station, fourteen miles from Little Rock, Ark., was murdered and robbed by an unknown assassin.

Gus Miller and Matthew Jones have been arrested at Kansas City, Mo., charged with inciting the mob of 1,000 persons which, on April 30, hanged Levi Harrington, colored.

An avalanche in Little Cottonwood, Utah, recently swept over the Richmond and Teresa mine, burying beyond reach to help Robert Greaves, the lessee of the mine.

The Pullman palace car shed and shop at New Orleans, together with three coaches and a large quantity of bedding and other supplies, burned on Saturday. Loss, $75,000.

Heavy forest fires are raging between Green Bush and the Black river, as far as Alcona, Mich. Unless rain comes speedily there will be great damage done to the pineries.

Daniel Johnson and Alfred Wright, colored laborers in the suburbs of Atlanta Ga., died suddenly returning from cutting outs. The men were overheated, and cooled off suddenly.

The League of American Wheelmen, composed mainly of bicyclists from New England and New York, meet to-day in Chicago. About two hundred delegates will be present.

A series of heavy thunder-storms occurred along the Hudson on Saturday. The Rochdale woolen mills, owned by the estate of Elias Titus, were struck by lightning and entirely destroyed. The loss is estimated at from $40,000 to $50,000; partially insured.

During a fight among bridge-builders at Hardeeville, South Carolina, on Saturday night, a colored man was killed by a white man, it is alleged, in self-defense. The negroes attempted to lynch the killer, but were prevented.

A banquet was given by the Commercial club of Chicago, on Saturday night, in honor of the commercial bodies of Cincinnati and St. Louis. 167 covers were laid, and the capital represented is estimated at $140,000,000. Among the guests were Postmaster General Howe and Lieutenant General Sheridan, and the latter "surprised the company by making an excellent speech of some length."

There is great excitement over Secretary Teller's decision opening the Turtle Mountain district. This region includes 9,000,000 acres of the finest land in Dakota, comparatively well wooded and watered, lying north and west of Devil's Lake. It has been closed hitherto by a claim of a wandering band of Chippewa Indians, now declared invalid. Two railroads, the Northern Pacific and the St. Paul, Minneapolis & Manitoba, will build into the region at once and thousands of settlers are ready to rush in as soon as it is formally opened.

Jesse Williams and Frank Miller, two burglars, entered the residence of H. P. Moore at night. The house was surrounded. Miller, in attempting to shoot down Mr. Henry Blackford, was cut down with a scythe. His head was partially severed, the tendons and arteries being cut through.

Ties were piled on the track between Hartford and Meriden, Conn., on Friday night and the Washington express train south was stopped by a watchman. There is a suspicion that this is another fraudulent trick of employees of the road, but nothing positive is known. The officials are investigating the matter.

In the supreme court of Washington county, R. I., a decree has been entered divorcing Catharine Chase-Sprague from William Sprague, giving Mrs. Sprague the custody of her three daughters and permitting her to resume her maiden name, with leave hereafter to apply for alimony if she chooses.

Willie Haley, of Pownal, Vt., aged 11 years, asked a friend how much poison would kill a boy. He was informed that three tablespoonfuls of Paris green would suffice. He took that amount of the poison and died next morning. His father killed himself a few months by cutting his throat and then hanging himself to a door latch. The boy had curly hair and was a handsome little fellow. He said he didn't want to live any more.

In Denver Phil. Hubbard, a jockey employed by Dick Mackey, a well known western horseman, met C. H. Wood, a real estate agent, and knocked him down and began beating him, when Mackey pulled Hubbard off. Upon arising Wood drew a revolver and began firing at Hubbard, hitting him twice. A stray shot struck John Denny, a Western Union telegraph repairer, passing through his thigh. It is thought by some that Mackey was also shot. He was driven away. Hubbard will probably die.

Committing Suicide With Poison.

In Eric, John Daley died suddenly on Thursday. He was believed to have committed suicide by taking poison. The friends of the family were indignant at the published report and said that Daley died a natural death. It was suspected that the true cause was being concealed to save insurance. The coroner was called and a post mortem held. A quantity of corrosive sublimate was found in the stomach and a verdict was rendered of suicide by poison.

What a Married Daughter Witnessed.

John Smith, an old California ranchman living near Milford, two hundred miles southwest of Salt Lake, quarreled with his wife, and seizing a double barreled shot gun, fired at her twice, both charges taking effect. He then coolly reloaded the weapon, went out of the door, fastened a string to the trigger, and placing the muzzle to his breast, fired six navy bullets into his body. He died two hours afterwards. A married daughter witnessed the tragedy. The old man was subject to fits of lunacy.

A Ball Dog Revolver's Work.

His last shot was fatal. The wife's injury is only a wound in the arm. It was the fourth time within a few years that Herr has attempted suicide—twice by poison and once by cutting his throat. Struck an Iceberg.
St. JOHN's, N. F., May 28.—The steamer Friary, twelve days from Newport, England, bound to New York, with iron and tin, put in here to-day for repairs. About noon Thursday, 800 miles east of Cape Spear, during a dense fog, the vessel struck an iceberg, carrying away bowsprit, figurehead, and smashing in ten or twelve feet of her bows, above the water line. Part of the berg, under water, penetrated the steamer's bottom, causing a large opening forward of the water-tight bulkhead. A diver this afternoon found the port bow stove from No. 9 to 20. No damage aft the bulkhead. The repairs will occupy two weeks. The royal mail steamer Plover arrived from the northward to-day. She encountered large quantities of ice in Green Bay, and had her bows badly damaged.

Base-Ball Games.

ALEXANDRIA, VA., May 28.—The game of base ball played yesterday afternoon on the grounds of the Episcopal High School, between the Howards and the Kendall nine, from the Deaf and Dumb College. resulted: Georgetown Howards, 15; Mutes, 6:

BALTIMORE, MD., May 28.—Cincinnati, 6; Baltimore, 1.

TROY, N. Y., May 28.—Worcester, 6; Troy, 4.

PRINCETON, N. J., May 28.—Brown University, 15; Princeton, 9.

PROVIDENCE, R. I., May 28.—Providence, 4; Boston, 1.

NEW HAVEN, CONN., May 28.—Howards, 10; Yale, 7.

"Good-Bye, Friends."

Boston, May 28.—The following was found by the harbor police in a bottle this evening:

St. GEORGE'S BANKS, March 10, 1882.—Fishing schooner Clyde: Our water has all run out, and we were dismasted by the fearful storm of the 8th inst., and as there is no vessel in sight, we expect to perish soon. This will not be thrown overboard until she is going down, so if you find this you will know we are all lost. Good-bye, friends.

Abraham Lincoln.

BROOKLYN, May 28.—Services in memory of Abraham Lincoln were held this afternoon at the monument at the entrance of Prospect Park in the presence of a large concourse of visitors. The monument was decorated with flowers.

The Sprague Property.

PROVIDENCE, May 28.—The trustee of the Sprague estate now advertise the property to be sold in parcels—the print works on the 29th of June and various parcels of real estate in this city on June 27 and July 1.

TELEGRAPHIC TWISTINGS.

—Yellow fever is raging at Havana at a frightful rate.

—Minister Sargent has been received at Berlin by the Crown Prince and Princess.

—The Novoe Vremya of St. Petersburg announces that General Albedinski intends to resign the governorship of Poland.

—Archbishop McCabe was enthroned as Cardinal with imposing ceremonies at the Catholic Cathedral in Dublin, on Sunday.

—Frank H. Stone and Arthur J. Cole, of Chicago, were drowned by the capsizing of their boat in Geneva Lake, Saturday.

—The lumbermen's association of Chicago increased the price of 1½ inch mixed lumber one dollar and timber joists and scantlings fifty cents.

—The Catholic clergy of London are about to commence preaching a crusade among the Irishmen of their flocks against connection with secret societies.

—Crickmore, Vanguard, Thora, Bounce, and Judge Murray were the winners at Pimlico on Saturday. French pools paid $5.00, $6.65, $7.10, $20,55, and 20.85.

—William C. McCamus, president of the Schenectady City National Bank, committed suicide by shooting, at midnight last night. Ill-health was probably the cause.

—George A. Conly, the wonderful basso, and Herman Rietzel, the pianist, of the Kellogg Opera Troupe, were drowned in Lake Spofford, New Hampshire, Saturday, while fishing.

—Bicyclists forming the League of American Wheelmen are now in Chicago to the number of 200, chiefly from New York and New England. They will hold a convention there, beginning to-day.

—Mrs. Susan Willis Fletcher, who was imprisoned in England on a charge of obtaining jewels from Mrs. Davis through alleged spiritualistic influence, reached New York Sunday on the steamer Celtic.

—The steamer San Juan, built for the Pacific Mall Steamship Company, was launched at Roach's yard Saturday. Her dimensions are: Length, 283 feet; beam, 36 feet; depth of hold, 25 feet, and tonnage 2,000.

—Ten Kickapoo Indians, living on a reservation in Atchinson County, Kan., were naturalized by the United States court at Topeka, and are now full American citizens, under the act recently passed by Congress.

—Fellowplay, Pinafore, Brother to Grimstead, Rochester, Bancroft, Bondholder, Hindoo, Lida Stanhope, and Maggie Ayer won at the Louisville races Saturday. Miss Malloy and Suananoa ran a dead heat in the last race—a Steeplechase.

—In an affray at Savannah, Ga., among the hands building the bridge over the Savannah at Hardeeville, S. C., a negro was killed in self-defense by a white man from Baltimore. The negroes attempted to lynch the latter, but were prevented.

—The French authorities in Tunis are greatly irritated by intelligence that Turkish troops have disembarked near the frontier between Tripoll and Tunis, in order to reinforce a camp already existing. The submission of the insurgent Arabs is now regarded improbable.

—P. T. Barnum sailed for Europe Saturday. To a reporter he said: "I'm going over with an eye to business. I intend to hire two and a half steamers from the Monarch line and take over the whole show next October. Bailey put me up to it. 'Bailey,' says I, 'the thing will cost $100,000,' 'What of it?' says Bailey; 'we'll take it in the first ten days.' Jumbo is to go along."

Edward Hanlan, the champion sculler of the world, arrived in New York Saturday from Liverpool on the City of Richmond. He does not like the idea of traveling to Manitoba for the next race, but thinks the inducement offered in the case of the match with Ross—$5,000 besides the stakes—sufficient to justify the trip. His future movements are uncertain. His friends in Toronto are getting up a reception for him, and he will shortly have to go there, but his stay in New York will extend over some days. Before leaving England he declined two offers, one of £1,000 for six months, the other of a like amount yearly for five years, to remain and give exhibitions and lessons in rowing.

These men belong to a gang of skilled mechanics from Baltimore, who were sent out to put in position the new iron bridge for the railroad over the Savannah river. There is also a large gang of negroes employed on the work, and latterly some of these have been very subordinate and turbulent. A number of them wanted to come up to Hardeeville on Saturday, and had made a request for the use of the hand car, which the Superintendent was compelled to decline, as it was the only one they had, and it was needed constantly. Notwithstanding this, they stole the hand car and went up to Hardeeville, which is about seven or eight miles distant. In the afternoon the two white men went up to Hardeeville to get their mail, and intended to return on the train. The negroes had been carousing about the place during the day, and many of them were under the influence of liquor. They encountered the white men in the evening, and were reprimanded for their conduct in taking the hand car. There was no difficulty that time, but later the negroes attempted violently to assault the white men, against whom, it seems, they have been harboring ill feeling for some time. The disturbance reached its height when the train arrived, and the white men, anxious to get away, attempted to pass through the crowd to reach the cars, when they were violently prevented, and one of them drew his pistol in self-defense and fired, with the result sta'ed.

ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A1:
SERIOUS ROW AT STRONG CITY.
The Outgrowth of Whisky and an Old Feud, Resulting Fatally to George Babb.
George Babb.

We learn from H. R. Fleetwood, who was one of a large number that went from this city to Cottonwood Falls last evening to attend the dedication of the colored Masonic lodge at that place, that a disgraceful and serious row occurred, in which G. O. Babb, a stone mason, was fatally shot. It seems that there is and has been an ill feeling for a long time between those living in Strong City and the Falls. Last night after the lodge exercises proper were over, the crowd dispersed and went over to Strong City, where a public installation of officers was had, which was followed by a dance in the hall. About eleven o'clock the trouble began, induced, no doubt, by the rather free indulgence in whisky, which fired the passions and renewed thoughts of the existing bad feelings between the two towns. As near as we have been able to get at the facts, one of the Falls boys tried to gain admittance to the dance without paying the requisite dollar. After the passing of a few harsh words with the door keeper, he was slapped in the face by the latter. This was promptly resented, and a general melee occurred, in which five persons received wounds. Word was dispatched for the sheriff, and in response Jabe Johnson hurried in the direction of the row. On his way there he received a shot in the hand, from a party he ordered to halt as he was on his way from the hall. It so happened that a construction train, with a large force of men was at Strong City, and they also mingled in the affray, pulling out for the west as soon as the affair was over. They are being pursued by Deputy Sheriff Johnson and posse of citizens. Early this morning Deputy Sheriff Cramer, of this city, received a telegram from Deputy Sheriff Johnson requesting him to arrest a certain party here, a negro who has been working for W. F. Ewing, under several aliases—Ben Ray being his real name. Cramer sought his man, arrested and placed him in jail to await the course of events. The man arrested here by Cramer acknowledges having been in the row, and narrowly escaped serious injury, a stray ball having passed through his pants leg. A small boy of Strong City received a bullet wound in the neck, but we learn none of the wounded five are badly injured. Excitement runs high at Cottonwood Falls, and it is not at all improbable that much trouble will result from last night's affray. The authorities think it unsafe for Ray to be taken away from this city for fear of mob violence. A large number of warrants have been issued, and several arrests will be made in the vicinity of the Falls.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A2:
DIDN'T FIND THEM IN.
A Gang of Armed Men Gather at the Chase County Jail.
To Avenge the Murder of Babb, but Find the Prisoners Flown.
By special advice from Cottonwood
To Avenge the Murder of Babb, but Find the Prisoners Flown.

By special advices from Cottonwood Falls, we learn that a mob numbering about one hundred and fifty, organized at Strong City Sunday, their purpose being to lynch the colored men, Ed. Bridges, Ben Ray, alias Scraggs, and Geo. Blakeman, who were in confinement at Cottonwood Falls on a charge of being participants in the serious row which lately occurred at Strong City, the particulars of which we have already published.

About ten o'clock at night information was given Sheriff Balch that such a mob had formed and with the above purpose. The sheriff at once set about to frustrate such a movement and with this view he procured a team, and securing the three culprits, set out for the jail at Eureka, Greenwood county. He had not been gone over ten minutes when the mob surrounded the jail, armed to the teeth, and called for the prisoners. Upon learning that they had been out-witted by the sheriff, and the birds had flown, no one knew in what direction, they were obliged to content themselves with loud words of imprecation and the discharging of their revolvers in the air. This, for the time, seemed to satisfy them, but finally becoming disgusted at not finding the prisoners, they dispersed.

Sheriff Balch is likely now in Eureka with his men, where they will be confined until the setting of the Chase county court, which will convene about the middle of May.

We are sorry that the citizens of Strong City should seek to take the law in their own hands, even though they consider the case an aggravated one, and hope that better counsels will prevail with them in future.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A4:
Taken to Cottonwood.
Last Sunday the sheriff of Chase county, in company with Deputy Sheriff Jabe Johnson, arrived in Emporia after the three negro prisoners implicated in the recent shooting affray at Strong City. They left on the 4 o'clock train this morning for Cottonwood, where Bridges and Blakemore will to-day have their preliminary examination. Ray was arraigned some time ago, when he waived examination, and in default of $8,000 bail was committed. The attorneys for the defense, so we learn, will ask for a change of venue, as they claim an im partial trial cannot be had in Chase county. The prisoners will doubtless now be lodged in the jail at Cottonwood, as matters have greatly quieted down, and no fears of mob violence are entertained. The trial of these men will not occur until the sitting of the Chase county district court some time in June.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A5:
THE BARB SHOOTING CASE.
Bridges Convicted of Murder in the Second Degree.
Messrs. Buck and Cunningham came in from Cottonwood Falls Friday, where they have been taking a silt in one of the murder cases there. It will be remembered that on April 4 the colored people at Strong City had a Masonic installation, supper and dance, and that one of the colored men named Alex. Blakeman and a white man named George Babb, being drunk, got into some fuss, and Blakeman slapped Babb in the face, for which Blakeman was at once tried and convicted of assault and battery and is now in jail for inability to pay the costs.

A half hour later in the evening some ten shots were fired on the sidewalk and in the street, and a colored man named Ed. Bridges got shot through the arm and across the breast. Another colored man by the name of Wes. Walker was shot in the hand, and George Babb received two shots, either of which were fatal, and died on the morning of April 8th. The coroners' jury decided that Walker, Bridges and Ray did the shooting of Babb. Walker ran away and the county attorney filed an informatoin against Bridges, Ray and Blakeman. Bridges tried to get a change of venue but failed. The papers at the time mentioned the organization of a mob to take the prisoners out and hang them. The county attorney, sheriff and some others brought the prisoners here and they were kept in our jail till May 8.

A nol. pros. has been entered as to Blakeman. Bridges has been tried and convicted of murder in the second degree. Motion for a new trial in his case is set for the 26th inst.

Six witnesses swore that Bridges fired the first shot and hit Babb, and six witnesses swore that Bridges had no weapon, did not shoot, and that Babb fired the first shot. The jury seems to have given the state the benefit of the doubt.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A8: Chase County Leader: A special session of court was held last Tuesday, with C N. Sterry as judge pro tem. A motion for a new trial in the Bridges-Babb murder case was argued and overruled, and Bridges was sentenced to the penitentiary for ten years, after which court adjourned until Monday.

Acquitted.
heretofore report
We have heretofore reported the litigation growing out of the killing of George Babb, at Strong City, April 4th, 1882. One Wes Walker, being advised that he might be roughly handled if caught, skipped out. Walker had been shot in the hand, Ed. Bridges in the arm and body, and Babb had received two wounds, either of which was mortal.

Bridges was tried in June last and convicted. His attorneys, Buck & Cunningham, have argued his case in the supreme court and expect a new trial. Ray was acquitted. Walker was recently arrested and bound over to court. On Thursday a jury was impaneled. Tom Jones, of Louisville, Miss., was shot and killed by F. L. Jones, a photographer of the same place, last Monday evening. From a private letter from Dr. G. Y. Jones had made the remarks he had attributed to him, whereupon F. L. Jones drew his pistol and fired upon him immediately. The shooting occurred in front of Dr. Woodward's store. Shortly before 3 o'clock this afternoon, one of the most terrible tragedies in the history of Leadville took place on upper Harrison avenue, the victim being Officer Samuel Townsend, one of the oldest and most popular officers of Leadville, and his slayer, Thomas C. Early, a leading young lawyer of this place. At the hour mentioned, the passers-by on Harrison avenue, near the corner of Fifth, were startled at the loud report of three pistol shots, one following the other in quick succession, and a thin, blue cloud of smoke, that curled and drifted from the hallway of the Union block, located the spot where one man stood with heated weapon clenched within his hand and another writhed in the agonies of dissolution. The crowd that hurried around the hallway were horror-stricken to see the well-known form of Officer Sam Townsend, the constable of Judge Talbot's court, prone upon the landing. Mr. T. C. Early was standing on the stairs, a few steps above, and paused, irresolute which way to go. His hat lay at his feet, and his clothing was disheveled, as though from a recent struggle. Fortunately among the first who were at the spot was Captain John Byrne, the detective in the city's employ, and taking in the situation at a glance, he placed Early under arrest, and hurried with him into Babcock's hat store next door. 'Ere this time the word that a murder had been committed, passed with lightning-like rapidity from mouth to mouth, and the pavement was blocked by a dense crowd that surged into the street and well nigh trampled one upon the other in their effort to reach the scene of the killing. As Byrne arrested Early, several gentlemen lifted Townsend up and carried him across the street to Dr. Dodge's drug store, where he was laid upon a pallet placed upon the floor, and Drs. Dougan and Gallaway were speedily at his side. He was suffering the greatest agony, and it was only with the greatest difficulty that he could be held down while an examination of his injuries was made. His garments were pulled open, and in the abdomen, about three inches above the right groin, a ghastly wound was revealed. The leaden messenger of destruction had buried itself in his bowels, and it was well nigh certain that death was only a matter of the briefest time. A messenger had been sent at once to his wife, and, with his little boy, she arrived in a few moments. The poor woman was scarcely able to realize the magnitude of the blow that had fallen upon her, and kneeling with streaming and agonized eyes by her husband's side, she pressed his hand convulsively to her breast, while the little one with great bewildered eyes stood holding to her dress. It was a sight that will never leave the memory of those who witnessed it.

The case that the quarrel grew out of was a replevin suit brought by a woman named Mamie Mordell against Carrie Adams, the proprietress of a Third street bagnio. Early represented the woman Mordell, and asked for a change of venue. This was granted, and Early claimed that Townsend had over-charged him in fees—a matter of ten or fifteen cents.

Judge Talbott says: "Townsend never either abused Early or threatened to whip him when in my court."

Irving Houser, the jeweler, took Townsend's gun out of its sheath after the shooting, and when it was prone on the landing. It had not been drawn. An eye-witness of the tragedy, a well-known citizen of Leadville, who is familiar with every shooting event in the bloody history of the camp, declares that the cold-blooded and deliberate determination with which Early shot Townsend has absolutely no parallel. The man took deliberate aim, and fired successively without the least sign of fear or trembling. His face, he says, wore an expression that can only be described as devilish in its murderous determination. Tucker's regime, a faithful and efficient deputy sheriff, and during all his official career demeaned himself in such a manner as to command the confidence, not only of his superiors, but the respect of all with whom his duties brought him in contact. By a series of reverses, however, he lost nearly all of his possessions, and at the time the calamity overtook him, to-day was, a comparatively poor man. He has a wife and a child, who were immediately notified of the distressing event, and at once hurried to the place where the unfortunate man was dying. Thomas C. Early, who formerly resided here, and who left Sedalia for Leadville, Col., some three years ago, at which latter place he has since resided, shot and killed a constable there on Monday. Public sentiment is strongly against Early, and the friends of the murdered man would surely have resorted to violence if permitted.

Thomas C. Early is well remembered by many Sedalians. He is a nephew of Gen. Jubal A. Early, of Virginia, and came to Sedalia some seven years ago. While here he married, and finally began the practice of law. He went to Leadville and became secretary of a mining company, and also practiced his profession. He had began to make money rapidly, and was active in politics.

j-c-early-leadville-1882-03-28.A12: Samuel C. Townsend of Leadville, Col., was brutally shot down in broad daylight, on the streets of that city, Tuesday, March 28. The trouble which led to the terrible deed grew out of a matter of costs in a justice court, Early claiming that Mr. Townsend had over charged him 10 or 15 cents. A dispute arose, and without warning Early drew a pistol from his pocket and fired at Townsend. Mr. Townsend endeavored to wrench the weapon from him. In the struggle the pistol was again discharged, the ball entering the abdomen of Mr. Townsend and lodging in the spine The wounded man lived only about half an hour. The murderer was soon under arrest. He claimed to have acted in self-defense only, but the testimony of two or three eye-witnesses, shows that Mr. Townsend did not strike the man nor attempt to shoot him, as Early claimed; and when he was picked up his pistol was found in his ulster with all its chambers loaded. Mr. Townsend was a native of Vermont. He was born in Wallingford in December, 1849; there he resided most of the time until 1871, when he went to Colorado and engaged in sheep-raising. In 1874 he was elected assessor and the year following sheriff of Rio Grande county, Colorado, afterwards serving as marshal of Del Norte and Alamrosa. In the latter town he married Miss Allie Allen, who, with one child, a boy, survives him.—Rutland Herald.

They quarrelled about the costs in a reprevin suit, in which Early acted as connsel. The latter forced the quarrel. The victim was unarmed and tried to get away. Shortly before 3 o'clock this afternoon, one of the most terrible tragedies in the history of Leadville took place on upper Harrison avenue, the victim being Officer Samuel Townsend, one of the oldest and most popular officers of Leadville, and his slayer, Thomas C. The crowd that hurried around the hallway were horror-stricken to see the well-known form of Officer Sam Townsend, the constable of Judge Talbot's court, prone upon the landing. Mr. T. C. Early was standing on the stairs, a few steps above, and paused, irresolute which way to go. His hat lay at his feet, and his clothing was disheveled, as though from a recent struggle. Fortunately among the first who were at the spot was Captain John Byrne, the detective in the city's employ, and taking in the situation at a glance, he placed Early under arrest, and hurried with him into Babcock's hat store next door. 'Ere this time the word that a murder had been committed, passed with lightning-like rapidity from mouth to mouth, and the pavement was blocked by a dense crowd that surged into the street and well nigh trampled one upon the other in their effort to reach the scene of the killing. His garments were pulled open, and in the abdomen, about three inches above the right groin, a ghastly wound was revealed. The leaden messenger of destruction had buried itself in his bowels, and it was well nigh certain that death was only a matter of the briefest time. A messenger had been sent at once to his wife, and, with his little boy, she arrived in a few moments. The poor woman was scarcely able to realize the magnitude of the blow that had fallen upon her, and kneeling with streaming and agonized eyes by her husband's side, she pressed his hand convulsively to her breast, while the little one with great bewildered eyes stood holding to her dress. A FORMER SEDALIAN
Kills a Constable in Leadville and is Rescued With Difficulty From a Mob.
Thomas C. Early, who formerly resided here, and who left Sedalia for Leadville, Col., some three years ago, at which latter place he has since resided, shot and killed a constable there on Monday. The dispute in which the constable was killed grew out of a law suit, in which Early was interested professionally, he being a lawyer. Early was immediately arrested and hurried off to jail, where he was placed under a strong guard in order to protect him from a mob which had gathered, and threatened to lynch the shootist. Public sentiment is strongly against Early, and the friends of the murdered man would surely have resorted to violence if permitted.

Thomas C. Early is well remembered by many Sedalians. He is a nephew of Gen. Jubal A. Early, of Virginia, and came to Sedalia some seven years ago. While here he became a reporter on the Sedalia Democrat, and latterly principal of Franklin school, which position he filled for one term only. While here he married, and finally began the practice of law. He went to Leadville and became secretary of a mining company, and also practiced his profession. He had began to make money rapidly, and was active in politics.

Electric Lamps.
If we examine one of the electric lamps in the street, we shall find it consists of two rods, one pointing upward from the bottom of the lamp, the other hangs downward. The rods seem to touch, and the brilliant flame is exactly where they seem to meet. Once a day a man comes around with a bag of the rods. He takes out the old rods that were burned the night before, and places a new set in each lamp. After he has gone about, as if he were putting new wicks into the lamps, and each is ready for its night work, all the lamps are lighted in broad day to see that every one is in proper trim. They are allowed to burn until men have walked about in the streets and looked at each lamp. If all are burning well, they are put out till it begins to grow dark. If one fails to burn properly a man goes to that one to see what is the matter. The rods are made of a curious black substance, like charcoal, that is called carbon. When the lamp is out, the two rods touch each other. To light the lamp, they are pulled apart; and if you look at the flame through a smoked glass, you will see that the rods do not quite touch. There is a small space between their points, and this is filled with fire. Look at the other parts of the rods, or the copper wires that extend along the streets. They have no light, no heat, no sound. The wires are cold, dark, and silent. If we were to push the rods in the lamp close together the light and heat would disappear, and the curious hissing would stop.

The electricity passes down one wire into the other, through the lamp, in silence and darkness, so long as the rods touch and the path is clear. When the rods in the lamp are pulled apart, there is a space to be got over, an obstruction, like rocks in the bed of the brook. The electricity, like water, struggles to get over the hindrance in its path, and it grows whitchot with anger, and flames and hisses as it leaps across the narrow space between the rods. There is another kind of electric lamp, used in houses; it has a smaller and softer light, steady, white and beautiful. In these lamps, also, we have something like the narrow place in the brook. They are made with slender loops of carbon, inclosed in glass globes. The electricity, flowing silently through a dark wire, enters the lamp, and finds only a narrow thread on which it can travel to reach the home-going wire, and, in its struggle to get past, it heats the tiny thread of carbon to whiteness. Like a live ecal, this slender thread gives us a mild, soft light, as long as the current flows. Never since I have been in this Territory has the law allowed a juror to be excluded on the ground that he has formed or expressed an opinion, and never so far as I know has one been excluded on such a ground. Indictments in Washington Territory are in the highest degree untechnical, and are by express statute made sufficient and have by the Courts been repeatedly held sufficient, if the act or omission charged as crime is clearly and distinctly set forth in ordinary and concise language, in such a manner as to enable a person of common understanding to know what is intended. Postponement of a criminal trial is a rare thing in this Territory, and is never granted without good cause shown, while expensive and protracted criminal trials, such as we once in a while hear of elsewhere, through the the press, are so far as I know things that never have occurred. Witnesses sometimes have to be brought great distances, and the mileage and per diem we pay is high, so that costs sometimes mount up to a considerable sum, but that is due to the sparse settlement of our immense domain and to our disposition to compensate well those whom we compel to attend our Courts.

By the records of this district it appears, that during the last twelve years—and I cannot go back further because the records are imperfect—there have been thirty persons arrested and indicted for homicide under the Territorial law; of these none that I know of escaped before trial except one temporarily, and only one was discharged without trial. Twenty-nine out of the thirty were tried. The trials of twenty-one came off within eight days after indictment. Two of the twenty-nine trials occupied four days, one three days and none of the rest to exceed two days. Only six continuances for one term were granted and three for two terms; one of the former because the jury disagreed; one because the prisoner was a woman great with child and could not be tried without endangering the life of her child as well as her own; one of the latter because at the first term the prisoner could not get his witnesses and at the second had escaped into British Columbia; and the rest by my predecessors for like adequate reasons no doubt. In the Senate, on the 9th, Mr. Call submitted an amendment to the Pensi- rears resolution providing for needy and disabled survivors of the Indian wars prior to 1845, including the Black Hawk, Creek and Seminole wars.

The editorial sanctum of the National Republican, Washington, D.C., was the scene of a tragedy on the night of the 8th. A. M. Soteldo, a committee clerk and newspaper man who had a grievance, called upon Clarence M. Barton, the managing editor, for redress. Pistols were resorted to, and Soteldo was fatally injured, the editor escaping with two slight wounds.

PITNEY, ex-Custodian of the Treasury Department, has revived interest in the contingent fund investigation by adding to his former testimony. He asked to be recalled, Feb. 9th, and stated that he had been informed that Upton and Lamphere had contradicted his testimony with regard to the employees of the Treasury having done work for Secretary Sherman, for which they were paid out of the contingent fund. He reaffirmed his testimony that they had done such work, and had been paid for it out of that fund, and said he was prepared to prove it, and also to prove that Secretary Sherman and Mrs. Sherman knew that this work was so paid for. Senator Hale sprang to his feet, and with some shout of indignation asked: "How dare you charge that Mrs. Sherman knew this?" Pitney replied: "I have received notes from her asking me to send men to do certain work on different occasions, and I have the notes here now." He then produced certain notes, proved to have been written by Mrs. Sherman, requesting that workmen be sent to the Secretary's residence. Pitney added that he had received notes of the same kind from Secretary Sherman, and also produced them.

A DISPATCH from Tombstone, Ariz., Feb. 8th, says the Coroner’s jury in the case of Wetzel, found murdered by Indians in Dragoon Mountains, charge the responsibility for that and similar offenses on the inefficiency and imbecility of the United States military authorities of the Territory. It is rumored that three more bodies of victims of the Indians have been found in the Dragoon Mountains.

JAMES Low, colored, of St. Louis, was so roughly treated by three of his own color in a Chicago gambling house the other night it was thought he would die. He was pounded with some blunt instrument which fractured his skull.

The following touching incident was telegraphed from Coalfield, Va., the scene of the recent mine horror, on the 7th: Superintendent Dodds mounted a coal car, and, addressing the walling throng of women and children around him, said: "My poor friends, it grieves me to have to state to you that for the present our search for the bodies of those you knew and loved will have to be abandoned. You know what fire in a coal mine means, and it may take months of watching to subdue it. We will close the pit now." The speaker's voice quivered with emotion. When he finished, a beautiful little girl of 14 years, Annie Crowder, the only daughter of one of the victims, uttered a piercing scream and rushed to the mouth of the pit, crying, "Oh, do not leave my dear papa to burn down there! Let me get in the cage and go down after him. Let me save him." The strong arms of the miners held her back as the fragile thing tried to make her way to the cage, and more than one blackened face was made blacker as the hand went up to wipe away the tears. Men sobbed aloud and turned away to conceal their emotion. The little girl, finding her progress barred, swooned at the mouth of the pit.

Having failed to execute some transportation contracts with the Government, James Callaghan, a prominent citizen of San Antonio, Tex., shot himself dead the other day.

FREIGHT trains on the Chicago, Minneapolis & St. Paul Railway telescoped, forty miles west of Eau Claire, Wis., on the 8th. George Winters, engineer, and a conductor were seriously injured.

GEORGE ROBINSON and Mary Baggan, of Chicago, were engaged to be married. On the 19th, Robinson called upon his sweetheart and sent a bullet into her head. He then placed the revolver behind his left ear and fired again, expiring immediately. The girl only lived a few minutes. Mary had refused to go out with Robinson the night previous.

Three murderers were executed on the 10th—Quirino Galtan, a Mexican, at Brownsville, Texas; Jesse Barber, colored, at Winnsboro, S. C.; Henry H. Hall, Prescott, Arizona. Charley Hing, a Chinaman, was hanged at Winnemucca, Humboldt County, Nev., on the 9th, for the murder of Ah Liek, one of his countrymen.

Eddie Kilberger, aged 12, pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the Common Pleas Court at Lancaster, Ohio, a few days ago, and was sentenced to the State Farm until of age. Young Kilberger stabbed a 12-year-old son of Christian Straacks to the heart one evening last October, during a quarrel about some marbles.

Judge Miller, of the United States Supreme Court, has issued a writ of error in the case of Charles F. Kring, sentenced to be hanged in St. Louis on Feb. 24th.

Five members of the Yeager family, of Fort Wayne, Ind., were recently poisoned by raw ham. It was not thought possible for the children to recover.

Two young men recently entered the works of the Chicago Car-wheel Company and asked some information from Walter Todd, the cashier. Almost instantly they threw red pepper in his eyes, pushed him into a closet, locked the door, and seized $400 in cash.

CLARENCE O. PERRY, a boy of 16, was recently left in charge of a house in Ashland, Mass., during the absence of the family. He set fire to three beds in different parts of the house, but the neighbors smelled smoke and extinguished the flames. The fellow was arrested and committed in $3,000 to await the Grand Jury's action. Perry is a monomaniac on the subject of incendiarism and confesses to at least three attempts.

WILLIAM LEDERE, of Syracuse, N. Y., loved Nellis Tait so passionately that he forced entrance to her residence the other day with the avowed purpose of killing her. The proprietress of the house tried to prevent this, and he shot both. He then went home and killed himself by emptying his revolver into his head. Jealousy.

Osborne Reaper Company for eighteen years and manager of the Chicago office for the last nine years, was found dead in the suburb of Hinsdale, Feb. 11th, brilt away between his house and the depot. The clothes and wallet had been rifled of their contents. He leaves a family in moderate circumstances.

Two coaches attached to an express train on the Wheeling & Lake Erie Railroad rolled into Huron River, about four miles from Huron, O., the other day. The train was going around a sharp bend on which the lower rail had probably been undermined by the recent high water. Thirteen persons were injured.

Five trackmen were killed in a tunnel on the Potomac Railroad, near the Union depot in Baltimore, Feb. 13, by a locomotive on the Western Maryland Railroad. The men were named David Grier, Timothy Kennedy, Edward Birmingham, James Irwin and Patrick McGoff. They stepped from one track to get out of the way of a passing train and walked directly in front of a locomotive on the opposite track.

AN OFFICER'S SHOT
Puts an End to the Existence of a Worthless Negro Convict at Overton Station.
He Tries to Brain Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler With an Ax. But Fails.
Yesterday afternoon Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler boarded a Cheasapeake and Ohio train for Overton station, in search of a negro named Bill Williams, an escaped convict from Eusley's plantation. Williams was arrested over a year ago for the shooting of Monroe Alexander, by Captain O'Haver and Sergeant Kuhnholtz. He was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. He worked on Eusley's plantation for several months, and finally made his escape. Before doing so, he set fire to a storehouse, which was

TOTALLY BURNED.

For six months the police have been looking for him, and information reaching them that Williams was in the neighborhood of Overton, the two officers, as already indicated, set out to catch him. Arriving at Overton Station, which is about six miles from here, they left the train and walked about three miles to the east until they came to the shanty of a negro named Cousins. Here they expected to find their man. Officer Butler approached the cabin and

TAPPED AT THE DOOR.

"Who's there?" came from within.

"A friend," said Officer Butler.

"You can't get in."

"Let me in."

"No, sir; the owner of the house told me to let nobody come in."

The officers held a short and decisive conversation. "Push in the door," said the sergeant. Officer Butler did as directed. The door yielded, and opened as it did so. Officer Butler saw the gleam of an ax in the air, and a blow directed at him cut the rim of his hat. He raised his pistol and

PULLED THE TRIGGER,

but the cartridge snapped and the negro bounded out and began slashing at Sergeant Scott with his murderous weapon. He cut the officer's pants with his ax, but did not hurt him. Seeing that the man was desperate and determined not to be taken, and the lives of both the officers being in danger, the sergeant coolly took aim at the negro and shot him. The criminal ran some twenty yards, and then, in the popular criminal language of the day, "fell with a dull thud." The officers held a rapid consultation. The negro was evidently dead, as they heard the

GURGLE IN his THROAT.

Knowing that it was a colored neighborhood and that the negroes would all be soon aroused, the officers started away as fast as they could, leaving the body. They heard the whole country howling shortly afterward, and they prepared to give the dusky recreants a warm reception if they had appeared. A Convict Shot.
MEMPHIS, January 15.—Jim Titus, alias Bill Williams, colored, a convict who escaped six months ago, was shot and killed this afternoon by Sergeant Scott, of the police force, while resisting arrest. The killing occurred ten miles north of Memphis.

LATESTELEGRAMS CONDENSED.
A receiver has been appointed for the World's Mutual Relief Association of Lebanon, Pennsylvania.

Three boys were instantly killed in Brook lyn, the other evening, by the falling of an unoccupied building, in which they were playing.

Hank Pruett, a Lake Erie & Western switchman, just recently married, was killed, at Lafayette, Indiana, last Friday night, while stepping in to pull a pin.

The bridge of the Chicago & Alton Road over Salt river, at Mexico, Missouri, went down with a freight train Saturday morning. Nobody, fortunately, was hurt.

A negro named White pawned an overcoat in St. Louis, Saturday night, and was arrested soon thereafter for stealing the same. He was locked up and the coat identified.

Eph Song, the young man who had a leg run over by a train the other day, just south of Winchester, Illinois, and whose leg was amputated, died Saturday from the effects of it.

Thomas Dolan, a section hand working on the Indianapolis & St. Louis road, just east of Pana, Illinois, was struck by the cars Saturday and seriously injured. He died soon after.

A Mrs. Diggins, whose relatives are among the ultra-fashionable in San Francisco, has just been discovered in criminal intimacy with her husband's friend, named Chase. A divorce, is pending.

General Logerot seized several notables at Stax as hostages for the payment of the war indemnity exacted by France. He threatens severe measures if the money is not forthcoming by the end of January.

Jim Titus, a colored convict; who escaped from Eusley's farm near Memphis, about six weeks ago, was shot and killed by Police Sergeant James Scott, a couple of days since. His whereabouts were discovered, but he refused to surrender to the officers, who thereupon shot him.

Two failures were chronicled on Saturday in Memphis, Tennessee. One of them was E. Lehman, retail clothier, who failed for $10,000, with assets about $5,000, and the other was Joseph Mulcahy, retail grocer, whose liabilities were $7,000; assets not known.

Three suspicious characters were arrested at Pana, Illinois, a few days since with a lot of shoes in their possession. They were detained by Marshal Rosenberry till Saturday, when officers from Madison county went after them, they having obtained the plunder by breaking into a freight car on the Chicago & Alton Road near Alton.

A man who passed under the name of William Wilcox made the acquaintance a few months ago of a girl named Mary Cregel, who was working at the Franklin House in Memphis, and succeeded in enticing her into a mock marriage. Two or three days since the whole thing was discovered, and the girl is almost crazy. Detectives are looking for Wilcox.

About 10 o'clock Saturday morning a young man named High Deman fell from the tower of the Union Depot, at St. Joe, Missouri, which he was covering, to the ground below. He fell fully thirty feet. His skull was fractured, one arm broken, a rib broken and other injuries sustained. He was taken up in an insensible condition and taken to the Lindell Hotel and medical aid summened.

An attempt to spread small-pox through the mails was reported to the postal authorities Saturday. An undated and unsigned letter, postmarked Cincinnati, was received by a farmer at Lynn, an office fifty miles north of Richmond, Indiana, in which two small-pox scales were enclosed. The letter read: "I have sent you the small-pox; go home and die." The letter was immediately burned, and the only clue to the perpetrator was thus destroyed, but the best detectives in the country will be set to work on the case.
Sedalia, Missouri, was a couple of days ago the scene of another tragedy. A number of workmen were engaged in erecting a large center-pole for a stone derrick, to be used in removing stone from railroad cars. The pole is about thirty-five feet long, two feet in diameter, and being green oak was very heavy. The workmen had just got the lower end of it into a deep hole and had the pole standing erect. One of the ropes which held it straight broke in two and let the log fall. It crushed Benjamin Ellis to the earth, and crushed him so bad that he died two hours later. Ellis leaves a wife and five children in destitute circumstances.

A fatal accident occurred Saturday afternoon at 1 o'clock on the Missouri Pacific Railroad, near Rose Hill, the first station west of Kirkwood, Missouri. A stranger, supposed to be a stone mason, had been looking for work on the St. Louis & San Francisco construction, and failing to get suitable employment, determined to return to St. Louis. The train was just passing when he got to Rose Hill. In attempting to get on board one of the cars he fell across the rail. A dozen or fifteen cars passed over him, cutting off both legs close up to the trunk. The sight was a horrible one. One leg was crushed out of all shape. The other was found some sixteen feet distant without a scratch upon it excepting where it had been severed from the man's body. Close by, between the rails, was the trunk. The unknown breathed his last as soon as the train men reached him. He was about 40 years of age, and the only paper found upon his body that might possibly lead to his identification, was a letter addressed to "Dennis O'Conol, Bartoid Valley P. O., St. Louis Co., Mo."

HAMPTON, Franklin County, Iowa, is much exercised over the discovery that the late County Treasurer, S. C. McKenzie, is a defaulter to the amount of $8,509. The Board of Supervisors are investigating the matter.

THOS. MORGAN, of Covington, Ky., while delirious from small-pox, jumped from a second-story window and crushed his skull.

A case of either lynching or very strange suicide has come to light near Churchville, Monroe County, N. Y. The body of a young man was found hanging by a halter from the limb of a tree. The man had evidently been dead but a short time. He was well dressed, and appeared to be about 26 years old.

Some seventy operators have been thrown out of work by the burning of a wool mill at Charlottesville, Va. The Adirondack Springs House, Whitehall, N. Y., burned. W. H. Collins, a fireman, was killed.

One seaman was drowned and two others probably fatally burned while fighting flames on the schooner Eugene, at Charleston, S. C.

THOMAS WATERS and Joseph Newton, of Oskaloosa, Iowa, were overpowered by foul air in a coal mine. The former died; the latter will not recover.

FRANK TAYLOR, of Napoleon, O., a Wabash employee, was run down by a yard engine at Toledo, O., and instantly killed.

TOPLIFF, an old resident of Alamakee County, Iowa, committed suicide by hanging.

A CHILD of J. B. Coles, residing near East Liverpool, O., died from drinking concentrated lye left within reach.

THE mother and daughter of John Nebb, a Newark (N. J.) saloon-keeper, were suffocated by a slight fire.

MAJOR HICKS, under sentence of death in the Covington (Ky.) jail, has small-pox.

A DISPATCH dated Yakima, W. T., 12th, says Toma Hop Towne, an Indian, was executed for the murder of Lorenzo D. Perkins and his wife. The murder was committed at Rattlesnake Creek, Yakima County, during the raid in the summer of 1878. Seven Indians were engaged in the murder. Three have been executed, three have been shot while resisting the Sheriff and endeavoring to escape jail, and one released, having turned State's evidence.

J. VAN ALSTEIN, of Princeton, Minn., resisting arrest, was killed by Policeman Turner, who was obliged to fire three shots, two of which took effect. Alstein was in liquor and attacked the officer with a bay-fork.

THADDEUS BABER and William Ward were hanged in St. Louis, Jan. 13. Moreau, the French-Canadian who killed his wife last September, was executed at Rimouski, Canada, on the same day. His head was nearly severed from his body. Joe Hay, Eidridge Scales and Matilda Carter, were hanged at Wentworth, N. C., for the murder of Nash Carter. All colored.

WM. MASON, Waupa, and Jos. Spain, Portage City, Wis., were both killed by runaway teams.

JOHN HAMER, Bucyrus, O., and Mike Riley, Waterloo, Iowa, were killed while coupling cars. The mangled remains of Sol. Davis, of Catlettsburg, Ky., were found on the track, where he had fallen asleep.

F. FRANK, a German farmer, was crushed to death under a load of wood at East Saginaw, Mich. His wagon was upset.

C. H. Gilbert, a farmer residing near La Grange, Ind., committed suicide by taking morphine. He had been drinking for some time and was under the influence of liquor when the deed was committed. He leaves a wife and two children, and was 40 years of age.

MISCREANTS near New Paris, O., removed a rail for the purpose of wrecking a Dayton & Western express train. The mail and express car was badly damaged. The fireman was seriously injured, but the passengers were unhurt.

BATES GALLAGHER was killed and Thomas Wade seriously injured by being thrown from a Cleveland & Pittsburg train near Steubenville, O. A truck became detached from the car.

THOMAS ALEXANDER, a highly respected citizen of Montgomery County, Ky. living in Stepstone, on the Big Sandy Railroad, was run over and killed by a passenger train. He was about 70 years old.

NEARLY the whole business portion of the village of Orwell, Out., was consumed by fire the other night.

MRS. NINNISS died in a dentist's chair at Grass Valley, Cal., while under the influence of chloroform. Everything was done to resuscitate her, but without avail. The Coroner's Jury in the case rendered a verdict that the woman came to her death from syncope, induced by chloroform, and exonerated Dr. Jones.

JIM TITUS, alias Bill Williams, a colored convict who escaped from Ensley's farm six months ago, was shot and killed by Police Sergeant James Scott, ten miles north of Memphis, Tenn., while resisting arrest.

The death is announced of Caroline Richings-Bernard, prominent in English opera some years ago.

She had forced him to sign a deed to the farm and taken the management of it herself. Then she refused to sustain the relation of wife to him any longer. She kept her agreement a few days and then hit him with a boot-jack for kissing her. This was supplemented by a severe thrashing, by the sons. Recently quarreling was renewed in consequence of the sale of a horse, by Daniel, the second son, and Mr. Smith disappeared. Knowing that the boys had threatened the old man's life, neighbors searched for the body and found it in a well, under nineteen feet of water and a pile of stones. There were two holes in the right temple, part of his clothes were torn off, and there were other marks of a scuffle. Investigation led to the discovery that he had been shot by Dan while sitting beside the kitchen fire, and the elder son helped to drag the body out to the barn lot and throw it in the well, while his wife stood guard and kept the smaller children locked up in a bedroom. EL PASO, August 17.—The Herald received the following special to-day from Socorro, New Mexico: Yesterday evening Juan Alvarid was arraigned before Judge Debaum, charged with rape, his victim being Eana Weldred, an 8-year-old daughter of John Weldred, a miner living here. The child is said to be dreadfully lacerated. Alvarid was bound over in bonds of $5,000, which he could not give, and was placed in jail. At night an immense crowd assembled around the jail and demanded the keys from the guard, which were given up after slight resistance. He was then taken in the presence of his victim, who identified him. The mob then marched him across the plaza to the rear of the Windsor hotel, when he was hung to a tree. He acted very courageously. When asked if he had anything to say he answered: "It's God's will and your wish; I die guilty, and am willing. Farewell to my friends." His body was cut down this morning at 8 o'clock. An inquest was held, the verdict rendered being: "Death from hanging at the hands of unknown parties."

HELL'S HOLLOW.
Another Calabasas Sunday Evening.

They had another shooting scrape at Calabasas Sunday evening. A gentleman who arrived in town Tuesday from that sinful hollow being approached for news by an Epitaph reporter, gave substantially the following facts: Igo's ranch is situated about twelve miles from Calabasas, on the line of the railroad. Sunday evening last some of the tough characters residing in the vicinity were "celebrating" the Sabbath at the camp of a Mexican living near Igo's. The Mexican had some women folks in his family, and the railroaders were making themselves particularly obliging to them. It may be that this was because of a natural spirit of chivalry for the fair sex, and it might have been because they were linguistic students, and anxious to master the soft, tender language of Castile, and then again, it might have been for causes not necessary to mention. At any rate the senoritas were having a good time. Mescal and whisky were plenty as water, and everything looked lovely. But mescal and whisky cannot be drank all day without its effects being felt, and it is as natural as life that railroaders should fight when their skins are filled with whisky. On this occasion four men, named James Moroney, Bill Mulcaby, Jack Kingsbury and a fellow called Nevada Jim, were candidates for the smiles of a certain senorita. Angry words came first, to be soon followed by blows. Pistols were then drawn, and Moroney received a ball in the forehead that sent him before his Maker almost instantly. This seemed to sober the others, and knowing that if the friends of the dead man arrived a serious row would ensue, they decamped in the direction of Calabasas. Arriving at that classic center, they forgot their trouble and entered into the festivities of a dance hall which was in full blast at the time. In the meantime, word of the killing near Igo's was wafted around quickly, and some of the dead man's friends organized a party to pursue the murderers. They followed on to Calabasas, and on inquiry learned that they were in the dance hall. They marched up to the door, revolvers in hand, and seeing the object of their search waltzing away gaily, turned loose their lead. A scene of dreadful confusion ensued. Not less than fifty shots were fired in half as many seconds. Yelling, cursing, screaming, moaning. the reports of firearms filing the air. During the melee the three chief criminals escaped by cutting their way through the tent. It must not be supposed that the pursuing party had the shooting all to themselves. Far from it; nearly every man and woman in the room took a hand in. When the ammunition was exhausted and the smoke cleared off, two men were found dead, and another, a Mexican, has doubtless died since. Four men and three women were wounded more or less seriously, but, as far as could be learned the three chief criminals escaped without a scratch. Of course their first thought was to escape the meshes of the law by crossing into Sonora, and thither they went. A consultation was held among the survivors at Calabasas, and it was decided to start a party on horseback after them. Twelve men armed to the teeth struck out about dusk, resolved to follow the fleeing fugitives into the heart of Mexico, or capture them. Neither the pursued or pursuing have been heard from since.

nevada-jim-arizona-1882-07.A11: News has reached this city, says the Tombstone Independent, that the pursuers of the three murderers who made Calabasas howl on Sunday night last, have returned, having accomplished what they went out for, the capture or death Bill Muleahey, Nevada Jim and Jack Kingsbury. In this case it was death to the trio. They were come up with some seventy-five or eighty miles over the border. When the fugitives saw their pursuers coming they took refuge within a bunch of scattered rocks that offered the only shelter on the open plain. Here a severe fight was made, during which the three murderers were killed and two or three of the pursuers were severely wounded. The dead were left on the ground they fell and the party returned to Calabasas where they were warmly greeted by the citizens of that lively burg.
