Bill Mulcahey, Jack Kingsbury and Nevada Jim, having killed two Mexicans and mortally wounded an American, at Albuquerque, N. M., were pursued by twelve men. They were caught up with at 4 o'clock on the 17th, the doomed desperadoes succeeding in reaching the reverses of the hill sides. The pursurers were received with a volley from Winchesters, and one of the vigilantes fell dead. Another assault was made. Two of the desperadoes, after a fierce battle, and the third Nevada Jim, was brought down with a ball in the thigh. The vigilantes spared his life till a rope could be had to hang him. The prisoner, however, suddenly seized a revolver from one of his dead comrades and shot Folley, a vigilante, dead. Laughing derisively he then shot himself.

Wm. Miller, overseer of the Woodstock, Conn., poor farm, was murdered by an inmate named Jake Parsons on the 20th. Miller requested Parsons to do some work on the farm, which so enraged him that he used a knife on the overseer with fatal results.

In a quarrel about a woman at Nashville, Teunn., on the 20th, Charles Blackmore was killed by Thomas Duling.

A coroner's jury investigating the suicide of Thomas W. Scott, at Little Rock, Ark., on the 20th, developed the fact that the deceased had murdered a man in Mississippi eight years ago and made his escape.

On Reques Plantation, near Cherow, S. C., on the 19th, William Hinson killed his wife.

John Carter, an English machinist, was murdered in a brutal manner at Chicago, by a man named McLaughlin.

James Long, who was brutally beaten by unknown persons at a dance given at Toronto on the evening of the 12th by orangemen, died from his injuries on the 19th.

Two years ago Dr. Roberts, of Ray County, Mo., was murdered by a young physician named Keyes who was jealous of the elder doctor's practice. The murderer pleaded insanity and was remanded to an asylum. On the 18th he returned to the scene of the tragedy, having been declared cured and discharged from the asylum. Charles Roberts, son of Keyes' victim, immediately sought out Keyes and shot him dead. Public sympathy is with Roberts as Keyes is said to be a bad character.

David I. Norwood, a prominent citizen of Floyd, La., attempted to cane L. J. Polk in the streets on the 18th. Pistols were brought into service, Polk being killed and his assailant severely wounded.

David Cook, a negro libertine, was lynched by masked men at the northern part of Kershaw County, S. C., on the 17th.

At the Texas Democratic State convention in Galveston a telegram was received from Governor Roberts declining to be a candidate for renomination. John Ireland was nominated for governor by acclamation.

A party of three women and four men were on the Portage river at Houghton, Mich., when the boat overturned, resulting in the drowning of two women and one of the men—Mrs. Joseph Blanchette and George Lacrosse and wife.

John Springer, aged 108 years, died in the county infirmary, near Marietta, O.

The Georgia Democrats at their State convention in Atlanta nominated a full ticket, headed by Alexander H. Stephens for governor.

J. R. Hagood, a prominent citizen of Warren county, N. C., and widely known throughout that State and Virginia, was crushed to death by being caught in the machinery of a wheat thresher.

At the Ohio Democratic State convention in Columbus the ticket nominated consisted of John W. Oakey, the present incumbent, for supreme judge; J. W. Newman for secretary of state, and Henry Weible for member of the board of public works.
During a fire in a shingle mill at Saginaw, Mich., two boilers exploded with terrific force. Two boys were instantly killed, and a number of men were hurt more or less seriously.

While a Mexican wagon train carrying 180 kegs of powder was going down a hill near Helena, Ark., some of the powder exploded. Two Mexicans and four mules were blown to pieces. Another man was blown to a height of 100 feet and killed.

A party of Arizona vigilantes in pursuit of William Mulcahy, John Kingsbury, and a notorious outlaw known as Nevada Jim, the murderers of two Mexicans, overtook them in a mountain ambushcade. A furious fight, in which rifles and revolvers were freely used, followed. Mulcahy and Kingsbury were shot dead, and one of the vigilantes was wounded. Nevada Jim was captured and told to prepare for immediate death. While the party were preparing a rope to hang him the prisoner snatched a revolver from one of them and shot himself through the brain.

Willard's bank, at Jonesborough, Ohio, has failed.
Glowing reports of the abundant harvests are continually received from nearly every point in the West.

The Indians are on the warpath in Arizona and have killed many of the whites, burned buildings, carried off or slaughtered stock and laid in waste the crops.

An unsuccessful attempt was made on a recent night to burn the town of Seattle, W. T. The attempt was evidently made by a brother of Payne, who was lynched last spring by the citizens of the place, and his gang of desperadoes. At the tap of a bell the vigilance committee assembled and hastily prepared a list of the names of twenty prominent "roughs," whom they ordered to leave the place before daylight or abide the consequences. The order was obeyed and the town was cleared.

SLEEPY EYE, July 13.—Seven boys, all between the ages of 12 and 18, were arrested here last night for plundering railway property. The oldest, Sommers by name, was examined on the charges of breaking open cars and taking goods; the others for taking goods. After an examination before a justice, Sommers, failing to give sufficient bonds, was committed to the New Ulm jail to await his trial at the next term of court. The trial of the others was adjourned to the 20th inst. Their operations have extended over a long period. For a long period a Pinkerton detective has been in town shadowing them, and last night he captured the gang without any trouble.

KILLED BY A JEALOUS HUSBAND.

COLLINSVILLE, Ill., July 14.—Last evening as John Dooler, colored, was riding through town on a mule, he was shot and wounded by Nelson Cooper, also colored. Dooler fell to the ground, when Cooper rushed up, placed his gun against the former's head and fired again. Dooler died and Cooper gave himself up. CALABASAS, A. T., July 14.—Two desperadoes were killed in Sonora by a pursuing party, a few days ago. The desperadoes took a hand in killing two men near Calabasas last Sunday.

BURIED ALIVE.

BRAINERD, July 14.—A terrible accident, attended with the loss of two lives, occurred here yesterday afternoon. Four men were excavating for the foundations of the new brewery, near the east bank of the Mississippi, south of the bridge, and had dug some distance into the bank, when a large mass of earth fell, covering them all. Two, who were nearest the outer edge of the superincumbent mass, managed to crawl out with but little injury. Workmen were soon on the spot, but it was

several hours before the remains of the other two men were reached. They were both dead when taken out. The victims were both single men, one of them being an American and the other a German. Their names are not known.

THE TEXARKANA HORROR.

TEXARKANA, Ark., July 14.—Nine more bodies were recovered from the ruins today. Most all were burned beyond recognition. One negro, found on the outside, and behind the building was removed from the rubbish. His body was not burned. Twenty bodies were buried this afternoon, business houses being all closed and citizens generally attending the funeral. Up to date twenty-eight bodies have been removed and it is supposed that a dozen others who were in the fire for thirty-six hours were completely cremated. Several men are missing and presumed to be among the dead.

Considerable damage was done to resident property in this city. A tree was blown across a school house seven miles south of here after school was out. Some damage was done to corn, but no fatalities are reported in the country as yet.

THEIR BOAT CAPSIZED.

KALAMOOZA, Mich., July 14.—At South Haven, last night, O. R. Foote, of the First National Bank of that place, and Miss Kittie Underwood, of Aurora, Illinois, were drowned by the upsetting of a sail boat. There was great excitement as both were popular. The bodies are not yet recovered.

FOUND AT LAST.

MILWAUKEE, July 14.—John Reilly, jr., 8 years old, who has been missing since July 12, was found drowned this morning.

ANOTHER BOY GONE.

A 5-year-old son of Edward Slattery, proprietor of the Clinton House, was drowned in the Milwaukee river to-day.

THE MOUNT PULASKI MURDERS.
Mount Pulaski, Aug. 22.—Charles McMahon, the farmer who with his hired men fell victims to assassins near here, was the owner of a splendid farm, where he dwelt in a quiet and retired way, as becomes a man of forty, and had accumulated a large fortune. He was a bachelor and did his own housekeeping, John Carlock, aged eighteen, and Bob. Matheeny, aged twenty, being the only other men about the place. Both were quiet and industrious, and like McMahon much esteemed. They were last seen on Thursday last week stacking wheat. The neighbors observing their their absence searched for them Saturday and Sunday and finally found all their bodies festering and offensively odorous in the rank weeds about the house. McMakon's throat was cut from ear to ear and his head almost severed from his body, the gash extending clear down to the spinal column and there was no shape to the battered head, about which a cloth had been tied. The bodies of Carlock and Matheney were covered with clotted gore and their throats cut as their employer's had been. Their limbs were bound securely with twine taken from the roofing machine, gagged and blindfolded with cloths. Everything pointed to the most fiendish determination and deliberate purpose. The house was ransacked, $2,000 in money taken and the household goods broken. A coroner's jury decided that the murder was committed by unknown persons, but the whole country is ablaze and on the alert. Lynch law will be inevitable if the murderers can be secured. Suspicion rests on a man who worked for the farmer some months ago, who was seen on the farm Thursday. Foot prints, as of two men, walking in single file, were discovered and followed two miles across lots until the trail was lost in the main road. There are no other clues, as the assassins had watered and fed the horses and taken other precautions to prevent discovery of the crime. They were no novices in the dreadful work. Jakie, who is suspected, is a tramping farm hand and quarrelled with McMahon about a year ago.

Monday morning at West Las Animas, Colo., two soldiers belonging to the troops at Fort Lyon had an altercation while in a drunken condition. Both men fired and one of them dropped dead; the other was arrested and placed in jail. Shortly afterward about fifty soldiers from the fort made their appearance and demanded the custody of the prisoner. The deputy sheriff in charge of the jail refused to deliver the murderer, wheroupon the leader of the soldier mob ordered his men to fire into the windows of the jail. Speedy Justice Done a Cold Blooded Murderer at Rock Creek.
Western Wyoming is the place for speedy and effective justice. Monday evening at Rawlins occurred another illustration of the way the ends of justice are met in the new west. A man named Gibbon, a hunter, according to advices received, entered the store of our former townsman, Chas. E. Clay, much the worse for the liquor he had taken in, and became embroiled in a wordy quarrel, during which he drew his revolver and shot down in cold blood one of Mr. Clay's three clerks, Robert Akin. The shot was a fatal one, for Akin died almost instantly.

Bystanders interfered too late to save the clerk, but gave the fellow a thorough mauling, when he was taken in charge by an assembled crowd, taken out to a box car near by, from the roof of which a plank was run out, fastened to the center board, and from this the offender Gibbon was effectually hung until dead.

Rumor also reached this city yesterday of another shooting affray at Ogalalla on the same evening, but inquiry over the wires disclosed the fact that the nearest that was come to this was a saloon war of words, in which numerous threats were scattered.

The remains of Robert Aiken the victim of Monday night's cold blooded murder at Rock Creek, passed east on yesterday's No. 4 en route to his home at Caliope, Iowa. Of him the Boomerang says: "Aiken, his victim, was a young man, and a favorite with the people of that section. He was never quarrelsome, and, as shown in the foregoing, his murder was entirely unprovoked. What renders his death all the more sad is the fact that he had just perfected arrangements for visiting his parents in the east, and reviewing the scenes of his boyhood days. Instead of a happy meeting with their son, the parents are now called on to mourn his untimely death."

WESTERN HUMOR.
A Spicy Account of Some Spontaneous Fun in Wyoming.
Wyoming Territory, so far from being the parent of but one funny man, is the home of humorists. She boasts of more humorists than Missouri has outlaws. In order to give the patrons of the paper published for the people now on earth an idea of our crude western humor, I'll quote from the meeting of humorists just recently held in the territory, and in order that said patrons may not too seriously criticize the style of humor, I will not say in both instances to which I am about to refer, the mirth-provoking fun was entirely extemporaneous.

Rock Creek, fifty miles west of here was the scene of the first meeting. A trapper entered the town during the forenoon, and, after disposing of his game, proceeded to bowl up. After placing 17 or 18 bowls to his credit, the humor in him began to extempore, and shortly afterward, in a fit of wild extemporaneous humor, he drew his gun, and, firing, instantly killed a young man, a citizen of the place. The citizens at once secured the humorist, bound him hand and foot and placed a guard over him, while a committee of humorists, for the purpose of taking immediate action in the premises, was being found, the committee formed. Many were in favor of sending the prisoner over the river by the way of the telegraph route, but this was objected to, and overruled. The chief argument being that said style of humor, like the Spoopendyke letters, was fast going out of fashion. After a further consultation, the committee decided to suspend the humorist from a box car which stood on the side track. This fresh out-burst of spontaneous humor was received with applause and the crowd of humorists proceeded at once to execute their plan. It was a grand success.

The coroner, after viewing the remains, gave out that it was his opinion that deceased came to his death by the breaking of his neck from falling from a box car, caused by the lack of rope.

The second meeting of humorists was held last Saturday at Fort Fetterman. The circumstances were very similar to the circumstances were very similar to the Rock Creek affair, differing only in the particular: The candidate for immigration, instead of going via the railroad route, climbed the golden stair through the foliage of a tall oak tree.

As I remarked before, Wyoming humor is mostly spontaneous. It's all extemporaneous, and we are always ready to extempore at the proper time. Very respectfully, ED. WALSH.

BALTIMORE, March 1.—This afternoon Robert Taylor, a colored convict in the Maryland penitentiary, was shot and killed by Prison Officer James Byrne. Taylor was employed in the foundry and was told by the foreman to go on another floor and make a casting in place of one he destroyed yesterday. He paid no attention to the foreman, when Byrne repeated the order. Taylor replied that he would not go on the other floor, and made an assault on Byrne, when the latter fired. Taylor grappled with the officer, and Mr. Thorne, the foreman, separated them. Taylor than ran for Thorne, but the latter escaped, and he returned to the assault upon Byrne, who fired two more shots, at the last of which Taylor fell and died within an hour. A jury of inquest rendered a verdict that the killing was in self-defense. Taylor was a powerful man, and at times very hard to manage.

The Attempted Assassination of Queen Victoria.
ARREST OF THE MAN WHO FIRED THE SHOT—ATTEMPTS
A cablegram in yesterday's Star announced the firing upon Queen Victoria last evening. A later dispatch from London gave the following particulars: As the Queen was entering her carriage this evening a man in the station-yard deliberately fired a pistol at her. The man, who was a miserable looking object, was immediately seized by several policemen and taken to the Windsor police station. No one was hurt. The man gave his name as Roderick MacLean. The Queen drove off to the castle immediately after she was fired at. The miscreant was followed to the police station by a large crowd of people. The prisoner was with difficulty rescued from the crowd. The Queen arrived at Windsor at 5:25 p.m. She had been in London since Tuesday, where she gave a drawing-room on Wednesday in honor of the Princess Helena, of Waldeck, who is to marry Prince Leopold. A crowd of people assembled at Buckingham Palace this morning in hopes that the Queen would drive out. The demeanor of the people was as cordial as usual. Newspaper hawkers are now (7:30 p.m.) crying the news on the London streets. It causes much sensation.

"There was a large crowd of spectators awaiting the Queen's arrival at Windsor. The Queen walked across the platform of the railway station to her carriage, which was waiting to take her to the castle. John Brown, her attendant, had already ascended to his seat behind the carriage, when a man standing at the entrance to the station-yard, among a number of spectators, pointed a pistol at the carriage and fired. To judge from the report the pistol was not heavily loaded. The Queen, who was probably not aware of what had happened, was immediately driven to the castle, but before she passed the man had been seized by the superintendent of the borough police, who was standing near by. He was also violently seized by the crowd, and was only rescued from them when three or four policemen came to the superintendent's assistance. The pistol was captured by one of the crowd. The prisoner, Roderick MacLean, who was miserably clad, was taken into High street and thence conveyed to the police station in a cab. As soon as the Queen arrived at the castle she ordered an equerry to proceed to the depot to enquire if any one had been hurt. The report of the pistol was sharp, but not loud. MacLean apparently intended firing again, when the revolver, which seemed to be a new one, was knocked from his hand by a bystander and handed to the police. Eton scholars were prominent in the attempt to lynch MacLean. The Right Hon. Sir Henry F. Ponsonby, the Queen's secretary, proceeded to the police station, and after obtaining all the information possible, telegraphed to Mr. Gladstone the facts of the assault. It is understood the Queen has not sustained any shock. MacLean is said to be an inhabitant of the South Sea and is twenty-seven years old. He states that he is a grocer's assistant. The doctors pronounce him sane. The revolver is a six-chambered Colt's, American make. Two chambers were found loaded, and two had recently been discharged. Fourteen ball-cartridges were found on the prisoner. MacLean says that hunger actuated the crime."

Robert Taylor (colored), a convict in the Maryland penitentiary, was shot and killed about 2 o'clock Wednesday afternoon in the foundry at the penitentiary by James Byrne, an officer of the institution. It appears that Taylor, the deceased, had imperfectly done some work the day previous, for which he had been reported by the foreman of the foundry, George W. Thorn, to Officer Byrne, who, under the regulations, sent Taylor to the office of Warden Wilkinson, where he (Taylor) was reprimanded, and told by the warden that he should do the work over after he had finished his task the following day (Wednesday). Accordingly, Wednesday about 1:45 P. M., Mr. Thorn, foreman of the foundry, ordered Taylor, as he had finished his task for the day, to make over the work which he had spoiled the day before. Taylor did not move, and deigned no reply to repeated orders to do the work. Thorn then reported the matter to Officer Byrne, who was in the foundry. That officer ordered Taylor to do the work as instructed by the foreman. Taylor still remained silent, and made no move to obey. Officer Byrne then told Taylor to "go into the office." Taylor said something about getting into trouble, and presently seized a molder's rammer and struck at the officer, who, simultaneously with the demonstration made by Taylor, drew his pistol. As the rammer (a hickory rod one and one-quarter inches in diameter, four feet long, with heavy iron mountings on both ends) descended, the officer threw up his right arm, pistol in hand, received the blow, discharging his pistol, which fell from his hand. The foreman (Thorn) ran up and seized Taylor from behind for a moment or two. Taylor freed himself from Thorn, whereupon Thorn retreated a few steps. Two other shots were fired by Officer Byrne, whose pistol had been returned to him by a convict who was present. Taylor, the colored convict, fell mortally wounded.

INGUAN CRUELTY.
The Brutal Treatment Inflicted Upon a Little Girl in an Illinois Town.

STERLING, Ill., Jan. 31. — It has been discovered that a man and woman named Seymour have been horribly maltreating a fatherless girl, seven years old, whom they were supposed to be taking care of. The child is small for its age, and Seymour compelled her to feed and take care of a horse and bring coal. He confined her in a cellar at times all day without food or clothing, except a thin dress, and punished her with a horsewhip until the surface of her entire body was black and blue and sore. Sometimes he would toss her to the ceiling and let her fall on the floor. No species of cruelty seemed too severe to adopt toward the child. The villagers last night made a determined though unsuccessful attempt to lynch Seymour, but both he and his wife have fled.

The village of Rock Falls, Whiteside county, Ill., was in a ferment on Monday. There lives in the place a Mrs Bolton, whose husband has been sent to the insane asylum, leaving her burdened with eight small children. A Times special thus tells the story:

About a month ago one of the children, a girl 7 years old, went to live with a man and woman named Seymour, and Saturday word reached the mother that her child was being abused. She went to Seymour's to inquire into the matter, and found the child in a horrible state from beating and starvation. The child was taken away, put under a physician's care, and warrants issued for the arrest of the guilty parties. Yesterday a great number of people visited the child, and the examination so maddened them that last night about 10 o'clock from twenty to thirty disguised men went to Seymour's house to lynch him. Word came to the man and his wife and they fled. The residence was searched and a number of other houses examined, but he was not caught. Returned Califormans said it looked like old times, and meant business. The child is small for its age, and Seymour compelled her to feed and take care of a horse and bring in coal. He confined her in the cellar at times all day without food or clothing except a thin dress, punished her with a horse-whip until the surface of the entire body was black and blue and sore, and would toss her toward the ceiling and let her fall on the floor. He prevented her going out doors more than once a day, and then when her clothes were soiled compelled her to clean them with her tongue. He insisted upon the child standing on one foot and then when the would become exhausted whipped her with a horsewhip. No species of cruelty seemed too severe to adopt toward the child. The people of the village are determined to have the fellow puished, and will leave no means tried that will reach that result.
